english_translation: Ancient kings lived in royal courts surrounded by stone walls.

dialogue.shona: Madzimambo ekare aigara mumizinda yakakomberedzwa nemadziro ematombo.
dialogue.english: Ancient kings lived in royal courts surrounded by stone walls.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Madzimambo [plural dzimambo] • ekare [ekare] • aigara [aigara] • mumizinda [in / singular mizinda] • yakakomberedzwa [it (past) komberedzwa] • nemadziro [and / with madziro] • ematombo [ematombo]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakakomberedzwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakakomberedzwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nemadziro'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nemadziro'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'madziro' forms 'nemadziro'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About How Things Used to Be: The '-ai-' Past Habitual ('aigara')
grammar_notes.content: In this sentence, 'aigara' uses the past habitual/imperfect marker '-ai-'. Whenever you talk about how people used to live in historical times, or an ongoing state in the past ('used to do', 'was/were doing'), Shona combines the subject prefix with '-ai-' + the verb stem: for example, 'vaigara' ('they used to live'), 'vaitengeserana' ('they used to trade with one another'), 'yaivakwa' ('it used to be built'), and 'hwaizivikanwa' ('it was renowned/known').
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -ai- + Verb Stem = 'used to [verb] / was [verb]-ing' (va- + -ai- + -bva = vaibva, 'they came from')

cultural_notes.title: Royal Capitals ('Mizinda yaMadzimambo') & Dry-Stone Architecture
cultural_notes.content: Across the Zimbabwean plateau—at Great Zimbabwe, Khami, Danamombe (Dhlodhlo), and Naletale—ancient rulers lived in elevated royal courts ('mizinda') encircled by intricately patterned granite stone walls ('madziro ematombo').

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Tora mvura uinwe.'
options: Put the cup on the table before you leave.
Close the window because it is cold outside.
Take the water and drink it.
Come here and help me carry the books.
active_exercises.correct_answer: Take the water and drink it.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you politely ask someone to speak softly ('taura zvinyoronyoro')?
Translate this new sentence into English: 'Mukoma wangu akatenga mota chena nezuro.'
options: My older brother bought a white car yesterday.
My sister is wearing a red dress today.
Which bus goes to the city centre?
The black truck is parked beside the road.
active_exercises.correct_answer: My older brother bought a white car yesterday.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Mukoma wangu' = 'My older brother', 'akatenga' = 'bought', 'mota chena' = 'a white car', 'nezuro' = 'yesterday'.
